essay:
Allen Toussaint's New Orleans sound was a system as much as a style: songs, arrangements, production, a small circle of independent-label operators, and a young rhythm section who could make the pocket feel both precise and loose. Toussaint's Minit years began in 1960, before he and A&R man Marshall Sehorn formed Sansu Enterprises in 1965. Sansu sessions, often made at Cosimo Matassa's studio, connected singers like Lee Dorsey and Betty Harris to Art Neville, Leo Nocentelli, George Porter Jr., and Zigaboo Modeliste—the musicians who took the name the Meters in 1968.

The playlist opens with the earlier Minit singles by Chris Kenner, Benny Spellman, and Irma Thomas, then follows the Dorsey/Toussaint partnership and Betty Harris's increasingly gritty sides. The central musical point is how the rhythm players shift between foreground and background: the soon-to-be Meters are a recurring studio nucleus, not a blanket credit on every Sansu session. James Black, for example, drums on Harris's “There's a Break in the Road.”

The Meters' 1969 debut makes that rhythmic grammar the lead voice, and their later “People Say” carries the story into the next room. Toussaint and Sehorn opened Sea-Saint in Gentilly in 1973; the Meters' 1974 album Rejuvenation was among the studio's first major projects. The arc therefore runs from a producer's early apprenticeship to an independent New Orleans studio family and a band that could stand on its own.

Sources: [64 Parishes — Allen Toussaint](https://64parishes.org/entry/allen-toussaint); [Signature Sounds — Sea-Saint history](https://signaturesoundsonline.com/people/music-industry-professionals/allen-toussaint-marshall-sehorn-sea-saint-studios/); [Indiana Public Media / Afterglow](https://www.ipm.org/show/afterglow/2019-09-11/world-allen-toussaint); [AllMusic — Betty Harris](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/betty-harris-mn0000049180).
